opus-5.5.text:
I think teleoperation has been incredibly valuable, and honestly a lot of the recent progress we've seen in robot learning comes from it. When you have a human operating the robot directly, the data is on-distribution for that robot's body, it's high quality, and it captures the kind of dexterous, contact-rich behavior that's really hard to get any other way. So I don't want to dismiss it at all.

But if the question is whether teleoperation *alone* can take us all the way, I'm skeptical. The core issue is scale. If you look at large language models, they were trained on essentially the whole internet, trillions of tokens. For robotics, even the biggest teleoperation efforts are collecting maybe tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of hours. That sounds like a lot, but it's orders of magnitude smaller. And teleoperation scales roughly linearly with people, robots, and time. You need hardware, operators, maintenance, and every hour of data costs real money. It's very hard to get the exponential curve we saw in other areas of AI from something that grows linearly.

There's also a diversity problem. Teleop data tends to be collected in a limited set of labs or staged environments, with a limited set of objects and tasks. A robot that will actually be useful in homes or factories has to handle a long tail of situations, and you can't send operators into every possible kitchen in the world.

So my view is that teleoperation is one important ingredient, but we need to combine it with other sources. Simulation is a big one. In sim you can generate enormous amounts of experience in parallel, and for things like locomotion we've already seen policies trained mostly in simulation transfer to real hardware very well. Then there's human video from the internet, which shows how people interact with the world even if it doesn't come with robot actions. And there's the knowledge already inside large vision-language models, which gives you semantic understanding and common sense for free. And eventually, once robots are deployed, they should be learning from their own experience through reinforcement learning, not just imitating humans.

I'd put it this way: teleoperation is great for bootstrapping and for teaching the fine-grained motor skills, but the scalable path is a mixture. Use teleop data efficiently, as the high-quality anchor, and let simulation, web data, foundation models, and autonomous self-improvement provide the scale. Whoever figures out the right recipe to blend these will make the biggest leap.

r001.rationale: It says teleoperation requires hardware, operators, and maintenance, and that every hour of data costs real money.

r002.rationale: It says the speaker is skeptical teleoperation alone can take robotics all the way and argues for combining it with other data and learning sources.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'm honestly skeptical that teleoperation alone gets us there. Teleop data is wonderful because it's real, it's in-distribution for the physical world, and it captures the kind of contact-rich nuance that's very hard to simulate. But the economics don't scale the way language or vision data scaled. On the internet, humans generated trillions of tokens as a byproduct of living their lives. Nobody is generating robot trajectories for free. Every hour of teleop data costs an operator's hour, plus the hardware, plus the setup, plus the failure cases you have to throw away.

So if you look at the numbers, even the most ambitious data collection efforts today are on the order of tens of thousands of hours, maybe hundreds of thousands if you're generous. Compare that to the scale of data that produced current language models and you're many orders of magnitude short. Linear collection doesn't close an exponential gap.

The second issue is diversity. Teleop data tends to be collected in a few labs, a few kitchens, a few warehouse mock-ups. The real world has an enormously long tail of objects, lighting, clutter, and physical variation. You can keep adding operators, but you're mostly sampling the same narrow slice over and over, and the policy's generalization reflects that.

My view is that teleop is a necessary ingredient but not the whole recipe. I think the scalable path is a mixture: simulation to get breadth and cheap variation, especially for locomotion and the things physics engines do well; internet video and human demonstration to learn priors about how tasks are structured; teleop to anchor everything in real contact dynamics and to fine-tune; and then, importantly, autonomous data collection where the robot itself generates experience, with teleop only for interventions. That last piece is what turns the data flywheel from linear into something closer to compounding, because the robot is working while it's learning.

So I'd say relying entirely on teleop is a bit like trying to train GPT by hiring people to type sentences one at a time. It gets you somewhere real, and we should absolutely keep doing it, but it's not the thing that scales.

r001.rationale: The response says teleoperation data does not scale economically because each hour requires an operator, hardware, setup, and handling failed cases.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the speaker is skeptical that teleoperation alone gets us there and calls teleop necessary but not the whole recipe.

astra-6.text:
I think teleoperation is a very useful way to collect data, but I’m skeptical that we can rely on it entirely to solve robotics. If every additional hour of robot experience requires an hour of human labor, collecting enough data becomes expensive. And it’s not just about the number of hours. It’s about covering different environments, different objects, and all the situations where something goes wrong.

Human demonstrations tend to show successful behavior. But a robot also needs to learn how to recover when it drops an object or ends up in a state that the human never demonstrated. You can collect demonstrations of those recoveries, but the space of possible failures is enormous.

So I see teleoperation as a starting point. It can teach the robot useful skills and give it a good initial policy. Then we need ways for the robot to improve through its own experience, whether that’s reinforcement learning in simulation or autonomous practice in the real world. The key to scaling is reducing how much human effort we need for each additional improvement.

r001.rationale: It says each additional hour of experience requires human labor, making enough data expensive.

r002.rationale: It expresses skepticism about relying entirely on teleoperation and says robots need to improve through their own experience.

sol-6.1.text:
I think teleoperation is a very useful way to collect data, but relying on it entirely is difficult to scale. Every hour of robot experience requires roughly an hour of human effort, and you need the robots, the operators, and the environments in which to collect that data. As you expand to more tasks and more situations, that becomes expensive.

There’s also a coverage problem. People can demonstrate how to perform a task successfully, but a robot needs to know what to do when something goes wrong—when it drops an object, loses its balance, or encounters something unexpected. Collecting demonstrations for all those situations is very challenging.

So I see teleoperation as an important starting point, rather than the whole solution. You can use demonstrations to teach the robot useful behaviors, and then use reinforcement learning and simulation to let it practice, explore, and improve. The key question is how much autonomous learning you can get from each hour of human demonstration.

r001.rationale: It says each hour of robot experience requires roughly an hour of human effort and that the robots, operators, and environments make collection expensive.

r002.rationale: It calls teleoperation a starting point rather than the whole solution and recommends autonomous practice through reinforcement learning and simulation.
